description.text: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BC in the town of Arpinum, a modest hill‑town southeast of Rome. Educated in Rome and later in Greece, he became a master of rhetoric and philosophy, translating Greek terms into Latin and creating a new philosophical vocabulary.
In 63 BC he was elected consul and famously exposed and suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy, delivering a series of speeches that have become classic examples of Roman oratory.

curiosities.text: He coined nearly 150 new Latin philosophical terms, such as evidentia, generator, and humanitas, enriching the Latin language with Greek philosophical concepts.
After his execution in 43 BC, Cicero’s severed hands and head were displayed on the Rostra, a rare public display of a senator’s body parts intended to warn others.
A substantial percentage of his work survives, making him one of the most important primary sources for the late Roman Republic and a lasting influence on Western thought.
